question.prompt: The solutions to the equation \((z+6)^8=81\) are connected in the complex plane to form a convex regular polygon, three of whose vertices are labeled \(A,\) \(B,\) and \(C.\) What is the least possible area of \(\triangle ABC?\)

solutions.title: Translate the roots and use coordinates
solutions.explanation:
The shift by \(6\) changes the location of the roots but preserves triangle areas. Set \(w=z+6\), so \(w^8=81\). These eight roots have modulus
\[
R=81^{1/8}=\sqrt3
\]
and arguments \(0^\circ,45^\circ,\ldots,315^\circ\). They form a regular octagon centered at the origin.

First, we justify why three consecutive vertices give the smallest triangle. Let \(s\) be the octagon's side length and \(d\) its shortest diagonal, which joins vertices two steps apart. Every triangle side has length at least \(s\). Also, three octagon vertices cannot all be pairwise neighbors, so at least one triangle side is a diagonal and has length at least \(d\).

For a triangle inscribed in a circle of radius \(R\), the sine rule and the sine area formula give
\[
K=\frac12 ab\sin C=\frac{abc}{4R}.
\]
Thus every triangle here has area at least \(s^2d/(4R)\). Three consecutive vertices have side lengths \(s,s,d\), so they attain this bound.

We can now compute the minimum using coordinates. Choose consecutive vertices
\[
A=\left(\frac{\sqrt6}{2},\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\right),\quad
B=(\sqrt3,0),\quad
C=\left(\frac{\sqrt6}{2},-\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\right).
\]
The vertical base \(AC\) has length \(\sqrt6\). Its line is \(x=\sqrt6/2\), so the perpendicular height from \(B\) is \(\sqrt3-\sqrt6/2\). Therefore the minimum area is
\[
\frac12\sqrt6\left(\sqrt3-\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\right)
=\boxed{\frac32\sqrt2-\frac32}.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
